title: Increase of Mean Inner Potential at Liquid Nitrogen Temperature of YBCO Using Electron Holography
content: Experimental evidence of superconductivity in cuprate superconductors has been possible due to the high critical temperatures (Tc), which exhibit electric current with zero resistance. Macroscopic evidence of superconductivity is the levitation of the superconductor on a magnet due to the Meissner effect is reached at relatively low temperatures [1]. The YBCO material discovered in 1987 was the first demonstration of a material to exhibit a high superconducting transition temperature (TC) of 90 K, nevertheless, the fundamental mechanisms able to support the experimental findings are not available so far. As a matter of fact, the superconductors that cannot be described by the Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer (BCS) theory are termed unconventional. This is the case for high-temperature superconductors such as YBCO. Hence, as the number of unconventional superconductors increases, a different physical mechanism will be required to support new observations [2]. In order to meet this need, an alternative to the BCS theory has been outlined by J. Hirsch, namely the theory of hole superconductivity [3], which applies to unconventional high-temperature superconductors. In the proposed theory, superconductivity is driven by a universal mechanism that is not related to electron-phonon interactions, but rather by electron-hole asymmetry. Following this principle, superconductors will expel negative charge from their interior towards the surface creating an internal electric field [4], which will be reflected on the mean inner potential (MIP) of the superconductor. The MIP is the volume-averaged electrostatic potential of a solid-state material which is dependent on the composition, crystal structure, and electronic configuration of the material of study [5]. Off-axis electron holography is an experimental method that enables to reconstruct and measure these phase shifts experienced by electrons when crossing from the vacuum to the surface of materials, this technique is ideal to characterize physical properties of materials since the electron wave is sensitive to magnetic and electrostatic contributions from the sample.
